newsitem.title: FRANCE: Eurotunnel to assess outlook, seek longer licence.
newsitem.headline: Eurotunnel to assess outlook, seek longer licence.

text.p: Eurotunnel SA/Plc plans to produce a prospectus shortly on the outlook in the coming years for the beleaguered operator of the sub-sea rail tunnel between Britain and France, co-chairman Patrick Ponsolle said on Saturday.

Ponsolle also said in an interview in the financial weekly Investir that he hoped for an answer by the end of the year to a request for an extension of Eurotunnel's licence to operate the Channel Tunnel, which would otherwise expire in the year 2052.

Ponsolle recently struck a deal with creditor banks designed to rid Eurotunnel of its debt troubles and secure its future but still has to win full support from its bankers and shareholders and a licence extension that would improve long-term prospects.
"The extension of the licence and greater confidence in the future of the company are vital to securing definitive backing from both sides," the French co-chairman told Investir.

The Channel Tunnel, a huge engineering feat, opened in 1994 and took on the ferry companies with sub-sea trains which carry cars coast-to-coast and also earns fees from railways offering a high-speed train service between London and Paris and Brussels, in competition with airlines.

But the massive debts run up building the tunnel and getting the service started brought it near financial ruin until the recent deal, which would alleviate its debt woes in return for giving creditor banks part-ownership of the company, at the expense of shareholders.
"A prospectus will be drawn up shortly for shareholders," Ponsolle said.

"I do not want to run ahead of the ball but we've already said we will easily increase turnover by at least 50 percent in 1996, despite a price war, at the same time as a rise of about 15 percent in operating costs," he said.

On the licence extension, Ponsolle said "We will submit a formal request to the British and French governments in the coming days. We hope for a reply before the end of the year. This would have a big psychological impact, especially on shareholders, but also the banks."

Eurotunnel's shares took a battering last week after they were requoted on the Paris and London stock exchanges in the wake of the debt deal which would give its 225 creditor banks 45.5 percent of the company in a debt-for-equity swap and could ultimately leave them with 54.5 percent of the capital.

The shares, which at one stage changed hands at 120 francs and were floated on the Paris stock exchange at 35 francs, slumped from nine francs when requoted on Tuesday to a low of 6.95 francs and ended the week at 7.90 francs in Paris, 95.5 pence in London.

The group does not expect to pay a dividend until after the end of the decade. Its immediate task is to get the provisional deal with its main banking negotiators agreed by the rest of the banks and also by the shareholders, many of them small-scale investors.
